glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: The Book of the Covenant closes with laws for honest justice and kindness even toward enemies, rhythms of rest that share God’s provision with the poor, three yearly feasts before the LORD, and His promise to send His Angel before Israel and give them the land little by little.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Exodus 23 completes the Book of the Covenant that began at 20:22. In chapter 24 Israel accepts these words and the covenant is sealed.

glance.label: Chapter Outline
glance.html:
• Exodus 23:1–9 — Honest Justice and Kindness Even to an Enemy

  • Exodus 23:10–13 — Rest for the Land, Workers, and Animals

  • Exodus 23:14–19 — Three Feasts and the Firstfruits of the Land

  • Exodus 23:20–26 — The Angel Who Bears the LORD’s Name Goes Before Israel

  • Exodus 23:27–33 — The LORD Will Drive Out the Nations Little by Little

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “‘Behold, I send an Angel before you to keep you in the way and to bring you into the place which I have prepared.” (Exodus 23:20)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Justice in Israel must be honest all the way down. No false report, no following the crowd to do evil, no tilting a case for the rich or even for the poor, and no bribes, “for a bribe blinds the discerning” (23:8). Justice comes with kindness. If an enemy’s donkey strays or collapses under its load, Israel must help. The stranger must not be oppressed, “for you know the heart of a stranger” (23:9).

God then orders Israel’s time. Every seventh year the land rests so the poor can eat, and every seventh day the animals, servants, and strangers are refreshed. Three times a year Israel gathers before the LORD for the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Harvest, and the Feast of Ingathering, and no one comes empty-handed. Worship shapes the calendar and confesses who gives every harvest.

Finally God looks ahead to the journey: “Behold, I send an Angel before you to keep you in the way and to bring you into the place which I have prepared” (23:20). This Angel bears God’s own name and authority, and He is probably an appearance of Christ. God will drive out the nations “little by little” (23:30), at the pace His people can hold the land, and Israel must make no covenant with their gods.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Exodus 23:1–9 — Honest Justice and Kindness Even to an Enemy

Israel must not spread false reports, follow the crowd into wrongdoing, twist justice for rich or poor, or take bribes. They must return an enemy’s straying animal, help the donkey of someone who hates them, and not oppress the stranger, since they know what it is to be strangers.

Exodus 23:10–13 — Rest for the Land, Workers, and Animals

Every seventh year the land lies fallow so the poor and the animals may eat, and every seventh day Israel rests so that animals, servants, and strangers are refreshed. Israel must heed all God has said and not even speak the names of other gods.

Exodus 23:14–19 — Three Feasts and the Firstfruits of the Land

Three times a year Israel keeps a feast to the LORD: Unleavened Bread, Harvest, and Ingathering, and no one is to appear before Him empty-handed. They are to bring the first of their harvest to the LORD’s house and not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk.

Exodus 23:20–26 — The Angel Who Bears the LORD’s Name Goes Before Israel

The LORD sends an Angel ahead of Israel to guard them and bring them to the place He has prepared, and they must obey Him because God’s name is in Him. If Israel obeys and rejects the gods of the land, the LORD will oppose their enemies and bless their food, water, and families.

Exodus 23:27–33 — The LORD Will Drive Out the Nations Little by Little

The LORD will send His terror and hornets ahead of Israel and drive out the land’s inhabitants little by little, until Israel grows enough to possess it within the borders He sets. Israel must make no covenant with these peoples or their gods, because serving them would be a trap.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Exodus 23 shows that justice and mercy belong together. The law forbids favoritism in court, even toward the poor, and in the same breath requires practical kindness even toward an enemy. God’s people are to be fair to everyone and kind to anyone.

The chapter also shows God’s care in the timing of His gifts. The seventh year and seventh day share His provision with those who have the least. The land would come gradually so Israel could hold it. The command about a young goat likely kept Israel’s harvest worship separate from pagan practice, reflected care for the order God made, and suggests that what God gives to nourish must never be turned to harm, like “the pure milk of the word” given to young believers (1 Peter 2:2).

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Honest justice. Israel must refuse false witness, crowd pressure, partiality, and bribes (23:1–3, 6–8).

Kindness to enemies and strangers. God’s people help an enemy’s animal and remember their own life as strangers (23:4–5, 9).

Rest that shares provision. The seventh year and seventh day refresh the poor, servants, strangers, and animals (23:10–12).

Worship that orders the year. Three feasts gather Israel before the LORD with thanksgiving for the harvest (23:14–17).

Guidance into the land. The name-bearing Angel goes before Israel, and God gives the land little by little (23:20–30).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Fallow (23:11). Land left unplanted for a year. Whatever grew on its own was left for the poor and the animals.

The three feasts (23:14–16). Unleavened Bread remembers the exodus. Harvest, later called Weeks or Pentecost, celebrates the first wheat. Ingathering, also called Tabernacles, celebrates the gathering of the year’s fruit.

A young goat in its mother’s milk (23:19). A command placed right after the firstfruits. It most likely separated Israel’s harvest worship from pagan practice and showed respect for the order God created.

My name is in Him (23:21). The Angel carries God’s own authority. In light of the bush (3:2–6), He is probably an appearance of Christ.

Hornets (23:28). Stinging insects, or possibly a picture of terror, that God would send ahead of Israel to drive out the nations.

focus: Exodus 23 completes the Book of the Covenant with laws for honest justice and kindness, rhythms of rest for land and workers, and three annual feasts at which Israel appears before the LORD. It closes with the LORD’s promise to send His Angel before Israel and to drive out the nations little by little, with a warning to make no covenant with their gods.

sections.title: Honest Justice and Kindness Even to an Enemy
sections.summary: Israel must not spread false reports, follow a crowd to do evil, pervert justice for rich or poor, or take a bribe, “for a bribe blinds the discerning” (Exodus 23:8). They must return an enemy’s straying animal, help the donkey of one who hates them, and not oppress the stranger, for they know the heart of a stranger.

sections.title: Rest for the Land, Workers, and Animals
sections.summary: Every seventh year the land is to lie fallow so that the poor may eat, and every seventh day Israel is to rest so that animals, the servant’s son, and the stranger may be refreshed. Israel is to be careful in all the LORD has said and not even mention the names of other gods.

sections.title: Three Feasts and the Firstfruits of the Land
sections.summary: Three times a year Israel is to keep a feast to the LORD: Unleavened Bread, Harvest, and Ingathering, and no one is to appear before Him empty. They are to bring the first of their firstfruits into the house of the LORD and not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk.

sections.title: The Angel Who Bears the LORD’s Name Goes Before Israel
sections.summary: The LORD sends an Angel before Israel to keep them in the way and bring them to the place He has prepared, and they must obey His voice, “for My name is in Him” (Exodus 23:21). If they obey the Angel’s voice and do all that the LORD speaks, He will be an enemy to their enemies; they must not bow down to the gods of the land but overthrow them, and as they serve the LORD He will bless their bread and water and take sickness away.

sections.title: The LORD Will Drive Out the Nations Little by Little
sections.summary: The LORD will send His fear and hornets before Israel and drive out the land’s inhabitants “little by little” (Exodus 23:30) until Israel increases enough to inherit the land, and He sets its bounds. Israel must make no covenant with these peoples or their gods, for serving their gods “will surely be a snare to you” (Exodus 23:33).

1.brief: Israel must not spread a false report or join with the wicked as an unrighteous witness. Truthful testimony protects justice.
1.explain:
“You shall not circulate a false report.”

Israel must not “circulate a false report,” spreading rumors or lies about another, especially in a legal matter. The ninth commandment (20:16) is applied to everyday speech and testimony.

“Do not put your hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness.”

To “put your hand with the wicked” means to join with them, perhaps by agreement. An “unrighteous witness” gives testimony that helps the guilty or harms the innocent. Truthful testimony protects justice.

2.brief: Israel must not follow a crowd to do evil or testify to pervert justice by siding with the majority. Justice must not bend to popular pressure.
2.explain:
“You shall not follow a crowd to do evil;”

Popular opinion does not make wrong right. Israel must not “follow a crowd to do evil.”

“nor shall you testify in a dispute so as to turn aside after many to pervert justice.”

In court, a witness must not go along with the majority to “pervert justice.” Justice must not bend to popular pressure.

3.brief: Israel must not show partiality to a poor man in his dispute. Even sympathy for the poor must not tilt a court’s judgment.
3.explain:
“You shall not show partiality to a poor man in his dispute.”

Even sympathy for the poor must not tilt a court’s judgment. A judge must decide by the facts, not by who the parties are. Leviticus 19:15 states both sides: do not favor the poor or honor the mighty.

4.brief: If they meet an enemy’s ox or donkey going astray, they must bring it back to him. Kindness is owed even to an enemy.
4.explain:
“If you meet your enemy’s ox or his donkey going astray,”

The law turns from court to daily life. Israel may come across an “enemy’s” animal wandering loose.

“you shall surely bring it back to him again.”

They must “bring it back.” Personal hostility is no excuse for letting a neighbor suffer loss. Kindness is owed even to an enemy.

5.brief: If they see the donkey of one who hates them lying under its burden, they must help him with it. Practical help must not be withheld because of hostility.
5.explain:
“If you see the donkey of one who hates you lying under its burden,”

The animal of someone “who hates you” has collapsed under its load.

“and you would refrain from helping it, you shall surely help him with it.”

Even if they want to walk past, they must “help him with it.” They must work alongside their enemy to free the animal. Practical help must not be withheld because of hostility.
5.notes: Proverbs 25:21 gives a similar instruction: “If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat.”

6.brief: Israel must not pervert the judgment of the poor in his dispute. The poor must receive justice and not be wronged.
6.explain:
“You shall not pervert the judgment of your poor in his dispute.”

The poor must not be denied justice. Verse 3 forbids favoring the poor. This verse forbids wronging them. Impartial justice protects both rich and poor.

7.brief: Israel must keep far from a false matter and not kill the innocent and righteous, “For I will not justify the wicked.” God Himself stands behind honest justice.
7.explain:
“Keep yourself far from a false matter;”

Israel must stay “far from a false matter,” any false charge or dishonest case.

“do not kill the innocent and righteous.”

A false accusation could send an innocent person to death. Israel must never let that happen.

“For I will not justify the wicked.”

God gives the reason. Even if a human court acquits the guilty, God will not. God Himself stands behind honest justice.

8.brief: Israel must take no bribe, “for a bribe blinds the discerning and perverts the words of the righteous.” Bribery corrupts even good judgment.
8.explain:
“And you shall take no bribe,”

Judges and witnesses must “take no bribe.”

“for a bribe blinds the discerning and perverts the words of the righteous.”

A bribe “blinds” even those who are wise and twists the words of the honest. Bribery corrupts even good judgment.
8.notes: Deuteronomy 16:19 repeats this warning almost word for word, adding “for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise.” God Himself shows no partiality “nor takes a bribe” (Deuteronomy 10:17).

9.brief: Israel must not oppress a stranger, “for you know the heart of a stranger, because you were strangers in the land of Egypt.” Remembering their own experience should shape how they treat outsiders.
9.explain:
“Also you shall not oppress a stranger,”

The command of 22:21 returns. Israel must not “oppress a stranger.”

“for you know the heart of a stranger, because you were strangers in the land of Egypt.”

Israel knows “the heart of a stranger,” what it feels like to be an outsider. They lived it in Egypt. Remembering their own experience should shape how they treat outsiders.

10.brief: For six years Israel is to sow its land and gather its produce. The land is to be worked faithfully in its season.
10.explain:
“Six years you shall sow your land and gather in its produce,”

For “six years” the land is to be farmed as usual. The land is to be worked faithfully in its season.

11.brief: In the seventh year the land is to rest and lie fallow so that the poor may eat, and the animals may eat what is left, and the same is true of vineyards and olive groves. The land’s rest provides for the poor and the creatures.
11.explain:
“but the seventh year you shall let it rest and lie fallow,”

In “the seventh year” the land rests. No crops are planted or harvested for profit.

“that the poor of your people may eat; and what they leave, the beasts of the field may eat.”

Whatever grows on its own is for “the poor.” What the poor leave is for “the beasts of the field.”

“In like manner you shall do with your vineyard and your olive grove.”

The same applies to vineyards and olive groves. The land’s rest provides for the poor and the creatures.
11.notes: Leviticus 25:1–7 develops the sabbatical year. The land belongs to God (Leviticus 25:23). 2 Chronicles 36:21 links the years of exile with the land’s neglected Sabbaths.

12.brief: Six days Israel works, and on the seventh it rests, so that the animals, the servant’s son, and the stranger may be refreshed. The Sabbath rest extends to everyone and everything under their care.
12.explain:
“Six days you shall do your work, and on the seventh day you shall rest,”

The weekly Sabbath (20:8–11) is restated.

“that your ox and your donkey may rest, and the son of your female servant and the stranger may be refreshed.”

Here the emphasis is on those who work for others: animals, the “son of your female servant,” and “the stranger.” They must be “refreshed,” able to catch their breath. The Sabbath rest extends to everyone and everything under their care.

13.brief: Israel must be careful in all God has said and not even mention the names of other gods. Faithfulness to God reaches even to their speech.
13.explain:
“And in all that I have said to you, be circumspect”

Israel must “be circumspect,” careful to keep everything God has said.

“and make no mention of the name of other gods, nor let it be heard from your mouth.”

They must not even “mention” the names of other gods, as in invoking them in oaths or worship. Faithfulness to God reaches even to their speech.
13.notes: Joshua 23:7 repeats this warning before Israel settled in the land.

14.brief: “Three times you shall keep a feast to Me in the year.” Israel’s year is to be ordered around worship of the LORD.
14.explain:
“Three times you shall keep a feast to Me in the year:”

Israel is to keep “three” pilgrimage feasts each year. Israel’s year is to be ordered around worship of the LORD.

15.brief: Israel must keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread in the month Abib, when they came out of Egypt, and “none shall appear before Me empty.” The first feast remembers the exodus, and every worshiper brings an offering.
15.explain:
“You shall keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread”

The first is “the Feast of Unleavened Bread” in spring.

“(you shall eat unleavened bread seven days, as I commanded you, at the time appointed in the month of Abib, for in it you came out of Egypt;”

The feast lasts “seven days” in the month “Abib,” remembering the exodus (12:15–20; 13:3–10).

“none shall appear before Me empty);”

No worshiper may come “empty”-handed. Each brings an offering in thanks for God’s provision. The first feast remembers the exodus, and every worshiper brings an offering.

16.brief: Israel must also keep the Feast of Harvest, for the firstfruits of their labor, and the Feast of Ingathering at the end of the year. The feasts thank God for each stage of the harvest.
16.explain:
“and the Feast of Harvest, the firstfruits of your labors which you have sown in the field;”

The second is “the Feast of Harvest,” at the beginning of the wheat harvest. It is also called the Feast of Weeks (34:22), and later Pentecost.

“and the Feast of Ingathering at the end of the year, when you have gathered in the fruit of your labors from the field.”

The third is “the Feast of Ingathering” in autumn, when the harvest is gathered in. It is also called the Feast of Tabernacles (Leviticus 23:34). The feasts thank God for each stage of the harvest.
16.notes: Leviticus 23 sets out the full calendar of feasts.

17.brief: Three times a year all Israel’s males are to appear before the Lord GOD. The men of Israel regularly come before God together.
17.explain:
“Three times in the year all your males shall appear before the Lord GOD.”

All the men of Israel must “appear before the Lord GOD” three times a year. The title “Lord GOD” stresses that the LORD is their Master. The men of Israel regularly come before God together.

18.brief: Israel must not offer the blood of God’s sacrifice with leavened bread or let the fat of His sacrifice remain until morning. God’s sacrifices must be offered as He directs.
18.explain:
“You shall not offer the blood of My sacrifice with leavened bread;”

Leavened bread must not be offered with “the blood of My sacrifice.” Leaven was excluded from offerings on the altar (Leviticus 2:11).

“nor shall the fat of My sacrifice remain until morning.”

The fat, which belonged to God (Leviticus 3:16), must be burned the same day. God’s sacrifices must be offered as He directs.

19.brief: Israel must bring the first of the firstfruits to the house of the LORD and must not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk. Following its placement after the firstfruits, the command most likely separates Israel’s harvest worship from pagan practice.
19.explain:
“The first of the firstfruits of your land you shall bring into the house of the LORD your God.”

Israel is to bring “the first of the firstfruits,” the very best of the earliest crops, to God’s house. God receives the first and best.

“You shall not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk.”

This command follows the firstfruits law. This study gives three reasons for it. First, its placement suggests it separates Israel’s harvest worship from pagan practice. Second, it reflects compassion and reverence for the order God created, like other laws protecting the bond between mother and young (Deuteronomy 22:6–7; Leviticus 22:28). Third, as a spiritual implication, it pictures the pure milk of the word, which must never be twisted to harm young believers (1 Peter 2:2).
19.notes: The command appears three times (23:19; 34:26; Deuteronomy 14:21). A damaged text from ancient Ugarit is often cited as evidence of a Canaanite ritual of cooking a kid in milk, but its reading is debated. It can be cited as support, not proof. Later Jewish practice developed the separation of meat and dairy from this command.

20.brief: God says, “Behold, I send an Angel before you to keep you in the way and to bring you into the place which I have prepared.” God promises guidance and protection all the way to the land, and this Angel is probably an appearance of Christ.
20.explain:
“Behold, I send an Angel before you to keep you in the way”

God promises to send “an Angel” to guard Israel on the journey. He will “keep you in the way,” protecting and guiding them.

“and to bring you into the place which I have prepared.”

The journey has a destination. God has already made ready the land He promised. He promises guidance and protection all the way to the land.

21.brief: Israel must beware of Him, obey His voice, and not provoke Him, for He will not pardon their transgressions, “for My name is in Him.” The Angel carries God’s own authority, so rebelling against Him is rebelling against God.
21.explain:
“Beware of Him and obey His voice;”

Israel must “beware of Him,” take Him seriously, and “obey His voice.” The journey depends on hearing and following Him.

“do not provoke Him, for He will not pardon your transgressions;”

The Angel “will not pardon” rebellion. He is not a mere messenger who can be ignored.

“for My name is in Him.”

The reason is decisive. The Angel carries God’s own identity and authority. To rebel against Him is to rebel against God. This Angel, like the Angel of the LORD at the burning bush (3:2–6), is probably an appearance of Christ before His incarnation. He bears God’s name and exercises God’s prerogative over sin.
21.notes: Isaiah 63:9 speaks of “the Angel of His Presence” who saved Israel.

22.brief: If Israel obeys His voice and does all God speaks, “then I will be an enemy to your enemies and an adversary to your adversaries.” God’s protection is tied to their obedience.
22.explain:
“But if you indeed obey His voice and do all that I speak,”

The promise depends on obedience. Notice that obeying “His voice” is the same as doing “all that I speak.” The Angel speaks God’s words.

“then I will be an enemy to your enemies and an adversary to your adversaries.”

God will stand against Israel’s enemies. God’s protection is tied to their obedience.

23.brief: God’s Angel will go before them and bring them to the peoples of the land, and God will cut them off. God Himself will deal with the nations Israel faces.
23.explain:
“For My Angel will go before you and bring you in to the Amorites and the Hittites and the Perizzites and the Canaanites and the Hivites and the Jebusites;”

The Angel will lead them into the land of the peoples listed.

“and I will cut them off.”

God Himself will “cut them off.” God will deal with the nations Israel faces. The judgment on the nations of Canaan was God’s judgment on long-standing wickedness (Genesis 15:16; Leviticus 18:24–25; Deuteronomy 9:4–5). It belonged to a specific moment in God’s covenant history and gives no warrant for violence by believers.

24.brief: Israel must not bow down to the gods of the land or follow their practices but must overthrow them and break down their sacred pillars. Entering the land requires rejecting its idols.
24.explain:
“You shall not bow down to their gods, nor serve them, nor do according to their works;”

Israel must not worship the gods of Canaan or copy their practices.

“but you shall utterly overthrow them and completely break down their sacred pillars.”

Israel must destroy the idols and “sacred pillars,” standing stones used in pagan worship. Entering the land requires rejecting its idols.

25.brief: “So you shall serve the LORD your God,” and He will bless their bread and water and take sickness away. God promises provision and health to those who worship Him.
25.explain:
“So you shall serve the LORD your God,”

Instead of serving Canaan’s gods, Israel must serve the LORD.

“and He will bless your bread and your water. And I will take sickness away from the midst of you.”

God promises to “bless your bread and your water” and “take sickness away.” The blessings Israel might seek from fertility gods will come from the LORD. God promises provision and health to those who worship Him (compare 15:26).

26.brief: No one will miscarry or be barren in the land, and God will fulfill the number of their days. God’s blessing extends to families and to long life.
26.explain:
“No one shall suffer miscarriage or be barren in your land;”

God promises fruitfulness in families. The people of Canaan sought children through their gods. Israel will receive them from the LORD.

“I will fulfill the number of your days.”

God will give full length of life. His blessing extends to families and to long life. These promises belong to Israel’s covenant in the land (Deuteronomy 7:12–15; 28:1–14). They show God’s goodness to an obedient people. They are not a guarantee that faithful believers today will never face sickness, barrenness, or early death.

27.brief: God will send His fear before them, throw their enemies into confusion, and make them turn their backs. God will fight ahead of His people.
27.explain:
“I will send My fear before you,”

God will send “My fear” ahead of Israel. The nations will be terrified of Israel’s God.

“I will cause confusion among all the people to whom you come, and will make all your enemies turn their backs to you.”

God will throw the enemy into “confusion” and make them flee. God will fight ahead of His people.

28.brief: God will send hornets before Israel to drive out the Hivite, the Canaanite, and the Hittite. God uses His own means to clear the way.
28.explain:
“And I will send hornets before you,”

God will send “hornets.” This may mean literal stinging insects or may describe the panic God sends on the nations.

“which shall drive out the Hivite, the Canaanite, and the Hittite from before you.”

They will drive out the peoples of the land. God uses His own means to clear the way.
28.notes: Joshua 24:12 says God sent the hornet before Israel, “but not with your sword or with your bow.” The Hebrew word occurs only here, in Deuteronomy 7:20, and in Joshua 24:12. Its exact meaning is debated.

29.brief: God will not drive them out in one year, lest the land become desolate and wild beasts multiply. The gradual conquest reflects God’s care for His people.
29.explain:
“I will not drive them out from before you in one year,”

God will not clear the land all at once.

“lest the land become desolate and the beasts of the field become too numerous for you.”

An empty land would be overrun by wild animals. Israel was not yet numerous enough to occupy all of it. The gradual conquest reflects God’s care for His people.

30.brief: “Little by little I will drive them out from before you,” until Israel grows enough to inherit the land. God gives the land at the pace His people can hold it.
30.explain:
“Little by little I will drive them out from before you,”

God will drive out the nations “little by little.” He sets the pace.

“until you have increased, and you inherit the land.”

As Israel grows in number, they will take possession of the land. God gives the land at the pace His people can hold it.
30.notes: Judges 2:20–23 and 3:1–4 add that God also left some nations to test Israel and to teach war to later generations.

31.brief: God sets Israel’s borders from the Red Sea to the sea of the Philistines and from the desert to the River, and He will deliver the inhabitants into their hand. The promised land has broad boundaries set by God.
31.explain:
“And I will set your bounds from the Red Sea to the sea, Philistia, and from the desert to the River.”

God sets wide borders: from “the Red Sea” to “the sea” of the Philistines (the Mediterranean), and from “the desert” to “the River,” the Euphrates.

“For I will deliver the inhabitants of the land into your hand, and you shall drive them out before you.”

God will give the land, and Israel will take possession. The promised land has broad boundaries set by God.
31.notes: The borders echo the promise to Abraham (Genesis 15:18). Israel reached something close to these limits under David and Solomon (1 Kings 4:21).

32.brief: “You shall make no covenant with them, nor with their gods.” Israel must not bind itself to the nations or their gods.
32.explain:
“You shall make no covenant with them, nor with their gods.”

Israel must not make treaties with the nations or their gods. A covenant with the people would bring their gods into Israel’s life. Israel must not bind itself to the nations or their gods.

33.brief: The nations must not dwell in Israel’s land, lest they lead Israel to sin, for serving their gods “will surely be a snare to you.” The warning closes the Book of the Covenant by guarding Israel’s exclusive loyalty to the LORD.
33.explain:
“They shall not dwell in your land, lest they make you sin against Me.”

The nations must not remain, because they would lead Israel into sin.

“For if you serve their gods, it will surely be a snare to you.”

Their gods would be “a snare,” a trap. The warning closes the Book of the Covenant by guarding Israel’s exclusive loyalty to the LORD.
33.notes: Israel’s later history proved the warning true. Judges 2:1–3 records the Angel of the LORD rebuking Israel for making covenants with the people of the land, saying their gods would be a snare.
